title: The Fed's biggest fear isn't tariffs—it's unanchored inflation expectations
dek: Chicago Fed President Goolsbee identifies the biggest risk as inflation: after five and a half years above target, the AI narrative may push rates up in the short term rather than down; his key advice for rate-sensitive industries is to watch the data, not the stock market.
why: A frontline policymaker rarely offers actionable quantitative anchors: the terminal rate is roughly 3%, but only if inflation returns to 2%; he also offers contrarian takes on the AI bubble and job-loss panic.
who: Founders, CFOs, and investors concerned about funding costs and interest rate trends; those planning AI capital expenditures or hiring decisions.
skip: The opening ad and Jackson Hole travel pleasantries (first ~4 minutes) can be fast-forwarded; the core is in the middle and later sections.

points.h: 19 chairs aren't for consensus—they're for argument
points.body: He explains why the FOMC is worth keeping with 12 regional Fed presidents plus 7 Board governors, totaling 19 chairs: not for consensus, but to let different worldviews collide in times of high uncertainty. Goolsbee says colleagues can shout at him or change his interpretation of the data. This structure insulates rate decisions from the political cycle as much as possible, because staggered 14-year terms mean no one can replace the whole table at once. The direct lesson for founders: when making major judgments, surround yourself with people who will push back, not an echo chamber.

points.h: The Fed's real fear isn't price hikes—it's unanchored expectations
points.body: The real danger of tariff and oil shocks isn't a one-time price increase, but making people believe high inflation will persist. Once such expectations form, workers demand 6% wages, businesses price at 7%, and the Fed must then use a deep recession to break those expectations. Goolsbee calls this 'unanchoring of inflation expectations' and says it's the self-fulfilling mechanism he watches most. For founders, this logic means: whether a cost increase is one-off matters more than how much costs rise.

points.h: Five and a half years above target—the Fed hasn't done well either
points.body: Goolsbee openly admits the Fed's recent performance hasn't been pretty: nearly six years, at least five and a half of them above the 2% target, with even a reversal in the last year. He cites on-the-ground observations from the Seventh District (the Midwest): businesses say input costs are soaring, farmers say prices can't keep up but costs are crushing, and everyone talks about affordability. His conclusion: with the public highly sensitive to prices, any new supply shock—tariffs, Middle East oil prices, chip shortages, AI data centers—is more easily interpreted as long-term inflation.

points.h: The new chair is pulling back the Fed's forward guidance
points.body: New Chair Kevin Walsh is overhauling the Fed's communication style: he dislikes 'forward guidance'—the explicit promise that 'if X happens, we'll hike or cut.' Goolsbee observes that FOMC statements have become noticeably shorter, and Walsh has set up five working groups covering inflation, AI and productivity, the balance sheet, and more, staffed with prominent names he trusts. Reports aren't out yet, but they could become Walsh's signature reform. Markets should adapt: the Fed will make fewer promises, and future expectation volatility may be higher.

points.h: Replacing people to influence rates is the red line for independence
points.body: Goolsbee divides today's pressures into two types: personal attacks on Powell, Lisa Cook, and others, including criminal investigations and attempts to remove them; and outright demands to 'cut rates.' He says Fed independence has traditionally been narrowly defined—setting rates free from political interference. Once an administration tries to influence rates by replacing people, 'any economist would see that as a problem.' He doesn't go all the way, but this is his clearest statement to the White House.

points.h: AI is a reason to hike rates in the short term, not cut
points.body: He first cools the AI narrative with district facts: manufacturing has the highest share in the entire Fed system, but firms are still looking for use cases and complaining that tokens are too expensive; productivity growth, after a two-and-a-half-year pickup, has shown about six months of weakness. Then he offers a counterintuitive judgment: if everyone simultaneously pours money into data centers, betting with IPOs or expected future earnings, the short-term economy could overheat. The central bank's daily job is to prevent overheating, not to judge whether AI will revolutionize things in 20 years, so AI's short-term policy implication may be to push rates up, not down.

points.h: AI taking all jobs is the lump-of-labor fallacy
points.body: He categorizes the narrative that 'AI will make everyone unemployed' as the lump of labor fallacy: treating the total amount of labor as a fixed stone that, once AI surpasses it, leaves people unable to find new work. He says this claim has been proven wrong every time in the past; he admits 'maybe this time is different,' but he's willing to bet the opposite: in 20 years, there won't be 95% unemployment, nor will only 6 people own all AI companies. He positions himself as a 'grim optimist'—not shying from short-term pain, but optimistic about long-term income growth.

points.h: The terminal rate is roughly 3%, provided inflation turns
points.body: Goolsbee offers a rare quantitative anchor: his personal loose view is that if inflation returns to a 2% path, rates will converge to the neutral rate (what he calls star), roughly 3% nominal = 2% inflation + 1% real. But the precondition is that inflation must turn downward; the past five and a half years have been above target, and the last year has been moving in the wrong direction. For rate-sensitive industries, his advice is to watch data and inflation, not the stock market—the people around the FOMC table discuss the real economy; the stock market is only a secondary reference.
